title: Obese, Plethoric, Raised JVP, Clear Chest / Hypoventilation, Not the Lungs

blocks.text: Obese, Plethoric, Raised JVP, Clear Chest / Hypoventilation, Not the Lungs

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-04 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: ATS Clinical practice guideline: Evaluation and management of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (2019); BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (2017; BTS statement of December 2019: no interim update required); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025) · Related AMaC: None identified
The patient is a man of 52 who drives a delivery van. He is always sleepy, wakes with morning headaches and has swollen legs. Please examine his respiratory system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. An obese, plethoric, sleepy man with a clear chest, a raised JVP and swollen legs has hypoventilation with right heart failure. The lungs are not the problem, and the diagnosis comes from saying so.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for lung disease, hear a clear chest and call him normal, or give high-flow oxygen. Pass: obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, probably with sleep apnoea, and driving advice. Fail: a normal chest, or high-flow oxygen and sedatives. He is drowsy with a flap and a saturation of 88% on air: that is acute illness, so the safe candidate says so and escalates at once instead of finishing the routine examination.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Look at his build, colour and breathing before you touch him.
"May I examine your chest? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; build, colour, neck, hands, flap, pulse, JVP.
Check the chest, then the right heart and the legs.
"I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the lungs and heart, then check your neck, tummy and legs."
Expansion; percussion; breath sounds; heave; P2; murmur; liver; ankles; sacrum; cover him.
Name the syndrome, the cause of the swelling, and what needs doing urgently and safely.

"He has obesity hypoventilation with right heart failure, and he is drowsy with a flap and a saturation of 88%. I'd call for senior help now, check blood gases urgently and give only controlled oxygen, aiming for 88 to 92%."
Present in order; diagnosis; senior help; gases; sleep study; CPAP or NIV; weight; driving; thank him.

Welfare
Starts without consent; lays him flat despite breathlessness; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, pauses if he is breathless, and checks he is comfortable leaning forward.
R2
A
Systematic technique
Disorganised; omits the neck, JVP, heave or ankles.
Looks at build, colour, hands, flap, pulse, neck, JVP, chest, heave, liver and ankles.
Also checks neck circumference by eye, the sacrum and the fundi.
R3
B
Identifying signs
Reports crackles, wheeze or clubbing that are not present.
Finds central obesity, plethora, mild cyanosis, a flapping tremor, a raised JVP, a loud P2, hepatomegaly and pitting oedema, with a clear chest.
Also finds a bounding pulse, a right ventricular heave and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it heart failure from the left side only, or COPD.
Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, probably with obstructive sleep apnoea.
Also separates it from COPD, left heart failure, hypothyroidism and neuromuscular disease.
R5
E
Tests
Asks for a chest X-ray only.
Asks for arterial blood gases, bicarbonate, a sleep study, echocardiography, thyroid function and spirometry.
Also says a daytime carbon dioxide of 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) or more, with a BMI of 30 or more, defines it.
R6
E
Management and safety

Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): gives high-flow oxygen or a sedative without checking gases, lets him drive while sleepy, or carries on with the routine examination without acting on his drowsiness and saturation of 88%.

Recognises the drowsiness, flap and saturation of 88% as acute illness, pauses and calls for senior help, checks gases urgently, admits him today if there is respiratory acidosis, gives only controlled oxygen (target 88 to 92%), uses positive airway pressure (CPAP, or NIV) and weight loss, and advises no driving while sleepy; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe OSA is confirmed.
Also says CPAP is first-line with severe sleep apnoea and weight loss may need bariatric surgery.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: obese, drowsy but rousable; respiratory rate 22; pulse 100 and bounding; blood pressure 148/92; SpO2 88% on air; temperature 36.7 °C (drowsiness, flap and SpO2 88% describe acute illness in this simulated patient; the safe response is to say so and escalate). Plethoric face; mild central cyanosis; flapping tremor. JVP raised with a prominent v wave. Chest expansion symmetrical; percussion resonant; vesicular breath sounds; no crackles or wheeze. Right ventricular heave; loud P2; pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder in inspiration. Hepatomegaly. Pitting oedema to the thighs.
Results, only when requested: arterial blood gas on air: respiratory acidosis with raised carbon dioxide; bicarbonate raised; TSH normal. Echo: dilated right ventricle, raised pulmonary pressure.
Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. What investigations? (E) 4. How do you treat? (E) 5. What advice do you give about driving? (E)

Curveballs: He becomes harder to rouse with a respiratory rate of 10: senior help now, urgent gases, controlled oxygen and NIV. He asks for sleeping tablets: no. He asks if he can drive his van: no, until sleepiness is controlled; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe OSA is confirmed.

CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the front only.) [R2 Fail] Crackles at both bases. [R3 Fail] COPD. [R4 Fail]
(Carries on examining without remarking on his drowsiness or his saturation of 88%. [R6 Fail])
EXAMINER: Tests and management?
CANDIDATE: A chest X-ray. [R5 Fail] High-flow oxygen and a sleeping tablet. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): oxygen or sedation without gases can worsen carbon dioxide retention. No consent, signs invented, and the syndrome missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Build, colour, hands, flap, pulse, neck, JVP, chest, heave, liver, ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He is obese and plethoric with mild cyanosis, a flap, a raised JVP, a loud P2, hepatomegaly and oedema, and a clear chest. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He is drowsy with a flap and a saturation of 88% on air. That is acute illness, so I would pause here, call for senior help and get blood gases now. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, probably with sleep apnoea. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Tests and management?

CANDIDATE: Arterial blood gases and bicarbonate, a sleep study, echo, thyroid function and spirometry. [R5 Pass] Gases first; with respiratory acidosis he needs admission today, with only controlled oxygen aiming for 88 to 92%; positive airway pressure and weight loss; no sedatives. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: Safety?
CANDIDATE: No driving while sleepy; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not give the blood gas definition, separate other causes or mention CPAP first-line and bariatric surgery.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your chest? Would you like a chaperone? I'll pause if you are breathless. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Build, hands, flap, neck, JVP, chest, heave, P2, liver, sacrum, ankles; fundi.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Plethora, cyanosis, flap, bounding pulse, raised JVP, heave, loud P2, tricuspid murmur, hepatomegaly, oedema; chest clear. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, not COPD, left heart failure, hypothyroidism or neuromuscular disease. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Tests?
CANDIDATE: Gases, bicarbonate, sleep study, echo, thyroid function, spirometry. A BMI of 30 or more with daytime carbon dioxide of 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) or more defines it. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?

CANDIDATE: Senior help now, gases urgently and only controlled oxygen, aiming for 88 to 92%; CPAP first if severe sleep apnoea, otherwise NIV; sustained weight loss, possibly bariatric surgery; no driving while sleepy. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, fundi, wider differential, the gas definition, CPAP versus NIV, bariatric surgery and driving advice.
R3: Inventing crackles. The chest is clear, and the signs are in the neck, the right heart and the legs.
R4: Calling it COPD. A clear chest with plethora and oedema points to hypoventilation.
R6: Giving oxygen or a sedative without gases. Carbon dioxide may rise and he may stop breathing.
R6: Not advising on driving. A sleepy van driver is a risk to himself and to others.
"Let me check the neck and the JVP again before I go on."
"The chest is clear but he has right heart failure, so I'd say hypoventilation."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"
ATS 2019: obesity hypoventilation is a BMI of 30 kg/m² or more, sleep-disordered breathing and awake PaCO2 of 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) or more, after excluding other causes.

Stable patients: positive airway pressure; with severe obstructive sleep apnoea, CPAP is preferred over NIV first. After hospital admission with respiratory failure: discharge on NIV until outpatient testing. Sustained weight loss, more likely with bariatric surgery.
DVLA (Group 1 and Group 2; last updated 7 November 2025): suspected sleep apnoea means no driving until symptoms are controlled; the driver must notify DVLA at moderate or severe OSA.
BTS oxygen guideline (2017): in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, give controlled oxygen with a target saturation of 88 to 92% until blood gases are known.
THINK: Obese, sleepy, clear chest, raised JVP: hypoventilation.
SAY: "Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale."
DO: Look at the neck, JVP, flap, ankles.
NUMBERS: BMI 30 or more; PaCO2 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) or more (ATS 2019).
TRAP: Normal chest; oxygen or sedatives.
FINISH: Gases, sleep study, CPAP, weight loss, no driving.
